title: UX Critique & Redesign: A Broken Signup Flow
prompt: A mobile app has a signup flow that users are dropping out of. It's a single long screen that asks, in order, for full name, email, password, phone number, date of birth, home address, and how you heard about us — with a generic 'Please fill all fields' error at the bottom if anything is wrong, and no way to see the password you typed. Walk me through how you'd critique this flow and how you'd redesign it. What's wrong, and what would you change?
blurb: A design-critique exercise — evaluate a flow against usability heuristics and real user needs, then redesign it with clear rationale and tradeoffs.

rubric.label: User empathy & needs
rubric.description: Grounds the critique in the user's goal and context (a motivated new user on mobile who wants to get in fast) and the emotional/cognitive cost of the current flow, not just aesthetic opinions.

rubric.label: Heuristic rigor
rubric.description: Systematically applies usability principles (visibility of system status, error prevention, clear error messaging, recognition over recall, minimal user input, match to real world) rather than ad-hoc reactions.

rubric.label: Problem prioritization
rubric.description: Separates the high-impact problems (asking for too much up front, unusable error handling) from minor ones, and reasons about which changes move the drop-off metric most.

rubric.label: Redesign quality
rubric.description: Proposes concrete, defensible changes (progressive disclosure / defer non-essential fields, inline field-level validation, show-password toggle, sensible input types/autofill, social/SSO option) tied to the problems found.

rubric.label: Tradeoffs & constraints
rubric.description: Acknowledges the business/data tradeoffs (the company wants phone/address/attribution) and negotiates them (defer, make optional, ask post-signup) rather than just deleting fields, and considers accessibility.

rubric.label: Communication & process
rubric.description: Structured critique, would validate with users/data (usability testing, funnel analytics, A/B test) rather than asserting, and communicates rationale clearly.

reference.scenario: Conversational design-critique at the mid bar. The candidate is given a deliberately bad mobile signup flow and asked to critique and redesign it. A strong candidate starts from the user and the goal — a motivated new user on a phone who wants to get into the product with minimal friction — then critiques systematically against usability heuristics rather than reacting aesthetically. The core problems: (1) it asks for far too much up front (seven fields, several not needed to create an account — phone, DOB, address, attribution), raising cognitive load and abandonment; (2) error handling violates 'help users recognize and recover from errors' — a single generic 'Please fill all fields' at the bottom gives no field-level guidance and no inline validation; (3) the hidden password with no show toggle causes entry errors (visibility of system status / error prevention); (4) likely missing input-type and autofill affordances (email keyboard, autocomplete), and no SSO/social option to skip typing entirely. The redesign applies progressive disclosure: ask only what's essential to create the account (email + password, or SSO), defer or make optional the marketing/profile fields to after signup or a later step, add inline field-level validation with specific messages, a show-password toggle and clear password rules, correct input types and autofill, and consider social login. Critically, a strong candidate negotiates the business's reasons for those fields (attribution, phone verification, compliance for DOB) rather than just deleting them — deferring, making optional, or explaining value — and mentions accessibility (labels, contrast, tap targets, screen readers). They close by wanting to validate: funnel analytics to see where drop-off actually happens, usability testing, and an A/B test of the redesign. Weak answers give surface aesthetic opinions, list random changes without heuristics or prioritization, delete fields without acknowledging why they exist, or never mention validating with users/data.
model_points: Start from the user and goal: a motivated new user on mobile wants to get into the product fast; every extra field and every unclear error is friction that competes with that motivation and drives abandonment.

Critique against heuristics, not taste: too much required input up front (Nielsen: minimize user memory/effort), poor error recovery (generic bottom-of-screen 'fill all fields'), no visibility of system status, no error prevention on the hidden password.

Prioritize by impact: the two biggest drop-off drivers are (a) asking for seven fields — several unnecessary to create an account — and (b) the unusable, non-specific, non-inline error handling. Fix those first.

Progressive disclosure / minimize the ask: require only what's needed to create an account (email + password, or SSO). Defer phone, DOB, address, and 'how did you hear about us' to after signup, a profile step, or make them optional.

Fix error handling: inline, field-level, specific, real-time validation ('Enter a valid email', password rules shown up front) instead of one generic error after submit; validate on blur, not only on submit.

Show-password toggle and clear password requirements up front to prevent errors and reduce failed submissions; correct input types (email keyboard, numeric where relevant) and autofill/autocomplete support.
Offer social login / SSO to let users skip typing entirely — often the single biggest conversion lever on mobile signup.

Negotiate the tradeoffs rather than just deleting fields: the business likely wants phone (verification), DOB (compliance/age), address (shipping), and attribution (marketing). Propose deferring, making optional, or collecting contextually when the value is clear — don't unilaterally remove data the business needs.
Accessibility: visible labels (not placeholder-only), sufficient contrast, adequate tap targets, logical focus order, and screen-reader-friendly error announcements.

Validate, don't assert: look at funnel analytics to see exactly which field/step drops users, run quick usability tests, and A/B test the redesign against the current flow rather than trusting opinion.

probes.question: Set aside how it looks — walk me through it against usability principles. Which heuristics is it violating and where?
The business added phone, date of birth, and address for real reasons — verification, compliance, shipping. How do you handle those instead of just removing them?
If you could only change two things to reduce drop-off, which two and why?
A user leaves one field blank and gets 'Please fill all fields.' What's wrong with that, and how would you redesign the validation and messaging?

probes.trigger: candidate never mentions the user's context
probes.question: Who is this user and what are they trying to do in this moment? How should that shape the flow?

probes.trigger: candidate asserts the redesign is better with no validation plan
probes.question: How would you know your redesign actually works and isn't just your preference? What would you measure or test?
How does this flow work for someone using a screen reader or with low vision? What would you change?

red_flags: Surface aesthetic critique with no reference to usability heuristics or user goals
Random list of changes with no prioritization by impact
Deletes fields the business needs without acknowledging or negotiating why they exist
Ignores the broken error handling / lack of inline validation
No mention of validating with data or users (analytics, usability testing, A/B)
Redesigns from personal taste rather than user needs and evidence
follow_ups: Product insists the phone number stays required at signup for fraud reasons. How do you make that as painless as possible?
Your redesign ships and drop-off barely moves. How do you find out why?
How would you decide between a single-screen form and a multi-step wizard here?
What would you test in a 20-minute usability session on this flow, and with whom?
How do you balance collecting marketing attribution against signup conversion?
reference.exemplar_answer: A strong candidate anchors on the user first: 'This is a motivated new user on a phone who wants to get into the app — every field and every vague error competes with that motivation, so my lens is minimizing friction.' Then a systematic critique: 'Against usability heuristics I see several problems. First, it asks for seven fields up front and most aren't needed to create an account — phone, date of birth, address, and how-you-heard-about-us are profile or marketing data, not account essentials; that's the biggest abandonment driver. Second, error recovery is broken: a single generic ''Please fill all fields'' at the bottom violates help-users-recover — it doesn't say which field or why, and there's no inline validation. Third, the hidden password with no show toggle and no stated rules causes avoidable entry errors.' Prioritized redesign: 'I'd require only email + password to create the account, or ideally offer social/SSO to skip typing entirely, and defer the rest to a post-signup profile step or make it optional. I'd add inline, field-level, real-time validation with specific messages, a show-password toggle with the rules shown up front, correct input types and autofill, and accessible labels and error announcements.' Tradeoffs: 'The business added those fields for reasons — verification, compliance, shipping, attribution — so rather than deleting them I'd defer them, make them optional, or collect them contextually when the value is obvious, and I'd bring the PM the funnel data to make that call.' Validation: 'I wouldn't trust my own taste — I'd look at funnel analytics to see exactly where users drop, run a few quick usability tests, and A/B test the redesign against the current flow.' The answer is heuristic-driven, prioritized, honest about business constraints, and evidence-seeking.

interviewer_notes: Run as a live critique. The strongest signal at mid level is a systematic, heuristic-driven evaluation grounded in the user's goal — not aesthetic reactions. Let them critique freely, then use probes to raise the bar: if they only talk about looks, force them onto usability principles; if they just delete fields, make them reckon with why the business added them; if they assert their redesign is better, make them produce a validation plan (analytics, usability testing, A/B). Reward prioritization by impact (the two big drivers are over-asking and broken error handling) and a redesign that ties each change to a specific problem. Check for accessibility awareness and for negotiating tradeoffs rather than steamrolling business needs. Penalize taste-based critique, unprioritized change-lists, unilateral field deletion, and asserting improvements with no way to validate them.
